title: Pinkerton: Pope Leo Reminds Europe Legal Is Not the Same as Moral – and Moral Matters More
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Pinkerton: Pope Leo Reminds Europe Legal Is Not the Same as Moral – and Moral Matters More

The general point of Christianity is that it’s about the spiritual, not the material—or the political.  As Jesus said in John 18:36, “My kingdom is not of this world.”

Actual Article Body:
The general point of Christianity is that it’s about the spiritual, not the material—or the political.  As Jesus said in John 18:36, “My kingdom is not of this world.”

Yet the worldly has a way of working itself in.  During Pope Leo XIV’s recent visit to France, he emphasized the Catholic Church’s teachings on such profound moral issues as abortion and “assisted” suicide (more like “compelled” in many cases).  And the visual tableau of the Pope comforting the afflicted but beloved Marie-Garance Nöel is more powerful and eloquent than a thousand-million-billion words.

The Pope said in France, “The motto of the journey was that the world may have life, and these words characterize the Gospel-centered nature of my meetings throughout the visit.”  That doesn’t sound very political, and yet the word “life,” alone, nevertheless does send a jolt.  And the Pope knows it: “I came to preach the Gospel,” he said, “if that’s politics, I did that.”

Still, the Pope is no pol.  Refreshingly above the grubby world of backrooms and bureaucracies, he summons us to God’s higher purposes, not lowest-common-denominator compromises.   As he puts it, “What is legal is not necessarily moral.”

Hmm.  So what if that distinction—legal vs. moral—were to get around?  What would change?  And what elected officials might be un-elected?

We can help answer those questions by benchmarking where we are today: The status quo of Western politics is constructed upon the idea of civic neutrality on values—and we need to think about what means today.

Pope Leo XIV blesses a child during the weekly general audience at St. Peter’s Square in the Vatican on September 30, 2026. (Massimo Valicchia/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The U.S. Constitution, for example, was written as a secular document, which is what the Framers intended: They wanted freedom of religion.

But they didn’t want freedom from religion.  As John Adams, our second president, wrote from the White House in 1798: “We have no Government armed with Power capable of contending with human Passions unbridled by morality and Religion.”

Adams and his colleagues figured that the small-government minimalism of the Constitution would be secure only so long as the citizenry’s personal behavior was guided by the morality of religion and related tradition.  If people comport themselves, there’s no need for fine-toothed statutes and lots of cops and judges and prisons.

Yet if internalized self-discipline is absent, Adams continued, “Avarice, Ambition, Revenge… would break the strongest Cords of our Constitution as a Whale goes through a Net.”  In other words, if people can’t manage themselves, government will have to be big enough to assert close control, because chaos is the worst outcome.  And if that happens, the experiment in limited government fails, and Americans lose their legitimate liberties.

“Our Constitution was made only for a moral and religious People,” Adams concluded.

So we see that the explicit civic neutrality of the Constitution always relied upon the implicit morality of the population.  The constitutional system works only if citizens fulfill their positive civic duty.

By contrast, a society with villains on the loose can’t have nice things, because the sidewalks, parks, and other public places will be a mess at best, and no-go zones at worst.  Everything else, too, goes haywire, from voting to volunteering.

Sadly, in America today, the political class has seen to it that much villainy has been legalized.  Some U.S. cities actually fund drug use and provide free housing for sex criminals.

Moreover, if any locality is spending money, it’s likely that the federal government is chipping in. The feds spend a trillion dollars a year on various welfare programs, many of which subsidize destructive behavior.

Which reminds us of the Pope’s wisdom: Legality isn’t the same as morality.  Let’s add: A fully legal policy or program might be immoral.
